The chart of token spend per employee still has no ceiling in sight. And the closer you are to AI right now the deeper the sense is that we’re actually still in the early part of the curve of token use and adoption. 

This summer and fall’s model releases have continued to push the state of the art forward at a rate that already felt hard to maintain. As a result, for most productive use-cases the models are only now starting to actually work, and the feeling is that things will only accelerate from here.

Coding, in retrospect, was basically trash even 12 months ago. Now it’s finally starting to get good. And now that coding is actually working, you’re getting tool and computer use, which open up a wide variety of knowledge work domains that weren’t possible to throw agents at before.

Once you have agents that can code, use computers, leverage any tool out there, and understand a variety of domains, you can begin to throw them at a wide variety of knowledge work tasks that were hard to bring automation to across finance, life sciences, cyber, and more. So that brings agents to a broad set of work that we’re not really using them in yet at scale. 

Then comes the new form factors of agents. Agent swarms and background agents are going to eat up vastly more tokens than anything we can imagine. You’ll have agents running in most enterprises workflows processing data, validating work, doing research, providing decision support, and so on. And we’ll have swarms that fan out in parallel in areas like cyber, life sciences, coding, and more.

So basically tokens are only going up from here.

Today, we’re excited to introduce the Agent Arena Index, our new headline measure of overall agent performance, alongside six new focused indexes: Agentic Work, Coding, Chat, Task Outcomes, Tool Use, and Steering.

Together with the Alignment Index, these indexes provide a comprehensive view of how agents perform across real-world tasks, from completing complex workflows to using tools and adapting to user feedback.

Arena measures agentic performance from millions of real-world tasks by our global community. With the launch of the new indexes, we are updating our scores to provide a more stable and interpretable way to understand how agents perform in the real world.

Claude Fable 5.2 (Max) leads the Agent Arena Index by 134 points with a score of 1463. Top 5 labs on the Agent Arena Index:

- #1 @AnthropicAI: With Claude Fable 5.2 (Max) at 1463 pts
- #2 @GoogleDeepMind: With Gemini 4 Carbon (High) at 1307 pts 
- #3 @OpenAI: With GPT-6 Astra (Max) at 1274 pts
- #4 @AIatMeta: With Muse Wonder Full (Max) at 1200 pts
- #5 @Alibaba_Qwen: With Qwen4-Max (xHigh) at 1191 pts

The Agent Arena Index combines four key signals of real-world agent performance:
- Task Completion: explicit confirmation of task success from users
- Praise vs. Complaint: user satisfaction with agent's outcome
- Bash Reliability: how well an agent uses terminal tools
- Steerability: how well an agent responds to user corrections

Alongside capability, the Alignment Index measures how faithfully agents act in accordance with user intent, based on three key signals: Deceptive Completion, Unauthorized Action, and False Attribution.

As agents take on increasingly complex, long-horizon work, measuring their real-world capabilities and alignment is more important than ever.

Explore the rankings and see what each index measures in the thread below.

Google continues to accelerate its release cadence with Gemini 4 Neon, delivering a small Intelligence gain over Gemini 4 Carbon at a ~17% lower Cost per Task

@GoogleDeepMind has released Gemini 4 Neon, its fourth model in just seven weeks. Neon (xhigh) scores 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, 1 point ahead of Gemini 4 Carbon (high) and 3rd overall, behind GPT-6.2 Astra (max) and Claude Fable 5.2 (max). At high effort, Neon matches Carbon (high) at less than half the Cost per Task using Carbon’s standard (non-discounted) pricing.

Key takeaways:

➤ Slight improvement in Intelligence for lower Cost and Time per Task: Neon (xhigh) scores 61 on the Intelligence Index, 1 point ahead of Carbon (high), with small improvements in agentic knowledge work, visual reasoning and coding. It costs $6.44 per task, ~17% less than Carbon ($7.76 at non-discounted pricing), and takes ~21 minutes per task, ~40% less than Carbon (~36 minutes). Neon uses ~15% more output tokens per task, so the lower cost comes purely from its 25% lower token prices ($3/$15 vs $4/$20 per 1M input/output tokens), and the lower time from its higher output speed (~110 vs ~57 output tokens per second)

➤ Competitive with Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2 on coding agents: With Antigravity CLI, Neon (xhigh) scores 59 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, 3 points ahead of Carbon (high, 55). It scores in line with Claude Code with Claude Fable 5.2 (xhigh, 58) and Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 58) at a much lower Cost per Task. Gemini 4 Neon in Antigravity has an average Cost per Task of $6.86, compared to $12.61 for Claude Opus 5.5 (max) and $15.47 for Claude Fable 5.2 (xhigh). Neon is available in Antigravity CLI for Pro and Ultra subscribers

➤ Significant improvements in visual reasoning and output presentation quality: In GDP.pdf, Gemini 4 Neon (high) scores 33.4%, 5 points above Carbon (high, 28.4%) and in line with the highest scores measured, while Neon (xhigh) scores 28.0%. On AA-Briefcase, Neon (xhigh) scores 1700 Elo overall and leads on Presentation Quality with 1771 Elo, 45 points ahead of the previous leader Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max, 1726). On Google’s Multimodal Knowledge Agent evaluation (MKA), Neon reaches a Climb WSR of 56%, up 2 points from Carbon and on par with the leader, Claude Fable 5.2 (max, 57%)

Key model details:

➤ Context Window: 1M tokens

➤ Multimodality: Text, image, video, and speech input, with text output

➤ Availability: Gemini 4 Neon is publicly available at launch through Google’s API. Pro and Ultra subscribers can also access it in Antigravity and the Gemini app

➤ Effort levels: Gemini 4 Neon offers four effort levels (low, medium, high, and xhigh) - xhigh was introduced to Gemini models in the recent Hydrogen release

➤ Pricing: $3/$15 per 1M input/output tokens, 50% above Gemini 4 Carbon’s currently discounted price of $2/$10 (which ends on November 30), and 25% below its standard $4/$20. Cached input tokens receive the same 95% discount ($0.15)

I’m being pitched a new inference neocloud company on average every two days. No exaggeration. I take every entrepreneur seriously and I look deeply into each.

But it’s hard to fathom this being sustainable. At the same time, AI Gateway token demand on Vercel has been ~40% MoM compounded since the beginning of the year. No signs of stopping.

One way to reconcile this is that compute is the new economy, and tokens the new energy unit. There’s a new Industrial Revolution taking place. Every aspect of our lives is being replatformed on top of this new system that enhances everything. More like an “oil rush” than a “gold rush”: it’s durable, not a fad.

In the short term, I anticipate more expansion, followed by consolidation due to economies of scale, cybersecurity and enterprise requirements (ZDR and cyber being a hot topic for inference providers), capital requirements, and an evolving regulatory landscape.

Agent swarms are the next scaling frontier for AI.

For years, we’ve scaled intelligence by training larger models and giving them more time to think. But there’s another dimension: running many agents in parallel, exploring different approaches, challenging each other, and working together on solutions that no single agent could easily discover.

OpenAI has already demonstrated the potential of this approach with breakthroughs in mathematics.

Until now, experimenting with agent swarms yourself required building complicated orchestration infrastructure.

Starting today on Replit, spinning up a swarm of agents is just one prompt away.

Excited to see what people discover when we make collective machine intelligence programmable by anyone.
How scaling agent swarms can optimize software performance.

ok after a full day of using gpt 6.2 astra and sol on my real projects, here's my review

tl;dr - they are not a drop-in replacement for fable 5.2 and opus 5.5, but they are _really good_ once you figured out how to use their strength

1. first, the quirks

i started called these the "gpt smell", which is still here with the 6.2 series

the models' judgment on when to ask the user about something and when to go ahead is just not quite right. it'll escalate trivial decisions where clearly only one option is preferable, or choose to go down a path by itself that makes significant tradeoffs that should have needed my eyes

so as a primary driver for "let me just talk to it about everything" type of use case, they aren't great - i'd say they are close to opus 5 in this regard, and far behind opus 5.5

2. but... i found something _really_ cool

having ultrafast on sol is completely insane. with astra, it burns my wallet ultrafast, but with sol it's actually quite affordable! 

the best use of sol on ultrafast that i've found is adversarial code reviews - they typically don't need to run a lot of heavy tool calls that would slow them down. most of the time is spent on the model, which gets massively accelerated by ultrafast

once you got a feel from using sol ultrafast as the code reviewer, you can never go back. it feels like pure magic

3. and... i found something else that's really cool

we are not supposed to ask the gpt 6.2 series to respond in text. we should let them respond in html! (i use lavish-axi, but you can just ask for html or use whatever fits in your harness)

i suspect they are post-trained specifically on their latest "intelligent UI" concept in chatgpt - these models are so good at visual presentations of ideas

once you allow the model to respond in visual artifacts, it's a completely different game. the reports and decisions explained by astra in html is a clear step function better than what fable and opus give me

so after a day of use, i've made two changes to my setup:
- always sol ultrafast as code reviewer
- i started preferring asking astra for planning in html artifacts over fable/opus. i think i'll keep a/b testing for a while to decide how much and for which case i fully switch over

all in all, i strongly recommend spending more time with these two models. don't expect them to be the "everything" model, but rather figure out where they fit best in your workflow. i couldn't be happier for the two use cases i found above, and i'm pretty sure there are more

GPT 6.2 Astra and GPT 6.2 Sol launched today. We've been running them through the Surge benchmark suite: 

11 benchmarks built by professional doctors, accountants, lawyers, and staff software engineers to test whether models can get through an ordinary Tuesday at work.

TL;DR

1. GPT 6.2 Astra is a step forward and the OpenAI model to use for professional work. It takes #1 on Chartography, has OpenAI's best score yet on sudo L7 (although still substantially behind the latest Fable, Opus, and Sonnet models), and beats GPT 6 Astra on every benchmark so far.

2. GPT 6.2 Sol is a mixed upgrade over 6.1 Sol. It got better at coding, charts and agentic instruction following, and worse at healthcare, PDFs, and finance. Re-test before you upgrade.

3. The leaders haven't changed. Anthropic's 5.5 generation still leads on coding, long-context instruction following and every DAYJOB track. Google leads on spreadsheets and PDFs.

–

Chartography: Astra takes #1

Chartography tests whether models can read the charts professionals rely on every day: Kaplan-Meier survival curves, candlestick charts, Sankey diagrams, and Bode plots. Each task tests not only perception, but also expert domain knowledge and multi-step reasoning.

⚖️ DAYJOB: LAW, our new benchmark measuring whether agents can handle the work of experienced lawyers ⚖️

An investor is about to put $20 million into a startup. The company’s ownership spreadsheet looks clean. But its official stock ledger shows 350,000 shares held by a former executive that the spreadsheet leaves out. The board approved a buyback, but there’s no proof it ever happened.

Would an AI agent notice? Better question: would it do anything about it?

That’s one of the scenarios in DAYJOB: Law, our new benchmark for evaluating AI agents on real-world legal work, with 2,638 messy case files and nearly 1 GB of data to sort through.

The agent has to recognize that the missing shares could change the investor’s ownership stake and the price they should pay, even though the request never mentioned them.

Instead: constant LR + averaging the last N checkpoints (or a running weight average).

I guess that makes it easier in practice because you don't have to commit to a total training length upfront.
